questions.stem: To what precision should burette readings be recorded?

options.text: To plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3, half the smallest 0.10 cm3 marking
options.explanation: Analogue instruments are read to half a division, so each burette reading carries the 0.05 uncertainty.
That discards the instrument's real precision.

options.text: To plus-or-minus 0.10 cm3 for each reading
options.explanation: 0.10 is the division size; the reading uncertainty is half of it.
No burette supports that claimed precision.

questions.stem: State the uncertainty carried by a single burette reading and by the titre.
questions.modelAnswer: A single reading carries plus-or-minus 0.05 cm3, and the titre, being the difference of two readings, carries plus-or-minus 0.10 cm3.

questions.stem: Describe how the aliquot is measured and delivered into the flask.
questions.modelAnswer: A volumetric pipette measures a known volume, usually 20 or 25 cm3, of one solution into the conical flask, with indicator added as drops.

questions.stem: Explain why the titre's uncertainty is double the single-reading uncertainty.
questions.modelAnswer: The titre is the difference of two burette readings, and uncertainties add when quantities are subtracted, so plus-or-minus 0.05 on each reading propagates to plus-or-minus 0.10 on the difference.

questions.stem: A student records final readings of 22.30, 22.40 and 25.80 cm3 against initial 0.00. Identify the concordant titres and the outlier to discard.
questions.modelAnswer: The 22.30 and 22.40 titres agree within 0.1 cm3 and are averaged; the 25.80 titre sits far outside the band and is discarded as the outlier.

questions.stem: State the four steps from titres to acid concentration.
questions.modelAnswer: Average the concordant titres, convert the standard's titre to moles, transfer moles through the equation ratio, and divide by the aliquot volume.

questions.stem: Write the equation for the reaction used in this core practical.
questions.modelAnswer: NaHCO3 + HCl gives NaCl + H2O + CO2, a one-to-one reaction between hydrogencarbonate and acid.

questions.stem: Explain why the standard solution's known concentration is the anchor of the whole calculation.
questions.modelAnswer: Every downstream number derives from the one quantity known exactly - the standard's concentration prices its moles, the ratio converts them, and the aliquot division finishes the chain, so an uncertain standard would corrupt everything.

questions.stem: A titre of 20.00 cm3 of 0.200 mol dm-3 hydrogencarbonate reacts with a 25.0 cm3 acid aliquot. Compute the acid concentration, showing each step.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles of hydrogencarbonate: 0.0200 x 0.200 = 4.00 x 10-3 mol; the 1:1 ratio passes them to the acid; concentration: 4.00 x 10-3 / 0.0250 = 0.160 mol dm-3.
